Can Statistics Detect Fake Data?

Identifying Anomalies and Outliers in Real Datasets Using Benford’s Law and Chi-Square Goodness-of-Fit

Shaik Sameer (24BDS1154) and Joshita Chowdary (24BRS1313)

19 October 2026

BOUNDARY STATEMENT (read before any result below). A statistically significant deviation from Benford’s Law is NOT proof of fraud, fabrication or manipulation. It is a diagnostic flag for further review. Legitimate explanations – constrained ranges, psychological price thresholds, caps, rounding and non-multiplicative processes – must be considered. This project reports statistically unusual first-digit patterns; it does not allege wrongdoing.

VIT Vellore – School of Advanced Sciences / School of Computer Science and Engineering

Course: BMAT202L Probability and Statistics (Theory) + BMAT202P Probability and Statistics Lab  |  Slot: F1

Faculty: Dr. Tharasi Dilleswar

Students: Shaik Sameer (24BDS1154)  ·  Joshita Chowdary (24BRS1313)

Stage: Review 2 → final deliverable (data cleaning in R, first-digit extraction, test statistic, diagnostics)

1 Executive summary

This report tests whether the first significant digit of nine curated World Bank World Development Indicators columns conforms to Benford’s Law \(P(d)=\log_{10}(1+1/d)\) using the Pearson chi-square goodness-of-fit test at \(\alpha = 0.05\). On the current run the analysis covered 627 analysis units (latest-complete-year cross-sections, pooled country-years, per-year subsets and per-region subsets) built from World Bank World Development Indicators (WDI) bulk CSV.

  • Pooled country-years: 5 of 12 indicators show a significant and practically material deviation, 0 show a significant but small deviation, 5 show no significant deviation, 2 were not assessed because the suitability screening rejected the column, and 0 were not assessed for want of sample.
  • Chi-square alone becomes oversensitive as \(N\) grows, so every result is reported together with the mean absolute deviation (MAD), the Nigrini conformity band, standardised per-digit residuals and Cohen’s \(w\).
  • A controlled synthetic manipulation experiment shows how the method behaves when a known fraction of records is altered; it also shows honestly that small, multiplicative alterations are hard to detect.

A significant result is a flag for review, not evidence of fraud.

2 1. Research question and objectives

Research question. Real datasets contain far too many numbers to audit by eye. Can statistics flag numerical data whose first-digit pattern differs from the Benford expectation?

Objectives.

  1. Select real, openly published numerical datasets with genuinely Benford-plausible columns.
  2. Prepare the data in R: import, type conversion, removal of aggregates, tidy reshaping.
  3. Explore the data (distributions, descriptive statistics, suitability for Benford analysis).
  4. Extract the first (and second, and first two) significant digits.
  5. Compute the Benford expected distribution from the formula - never from the data.
  6. Test the observed distribution against the expected one with the chi-square goodness-of-fit statistic, including the validity conditions for the test.
  7. Flag anomalies using a transparent, pre-declared rule that combines significance with a practical effect-size measure.
  8. Interpret the output carefully, with the established boundary that deviation is not fraud, and quantify how well (and how badly) the method detects known alteration in a controlled synthetic experiment.

2.1 1.1 The eight-stage flow (fixed in Review 1)

  1. Dataset selection  2.  Data preparation in R  3.  Exploratory analysis  4.  First-digit extraction  5.  Benford expected distribution  6.  Chi-square goodness-of-fit  7.  Anomaly flagging  8.  Interpretation.

5 4. Methodology

5.1 4.1 The Benford reference distribution

For the first significant digit \(d \in \{1,\dots,9\}\),

\[P(d) = \log_{10}\!\left(1 + \frac{1}{d}\right), \qquad E(d) = N \cdot P(d).\]

The expected proportions and the Review-1 reference example are reproduced below straight from outputs/tables/benford_expected_probabilities.csv, and the code derives them from the formula (they are never read from the data).

Benford first-digit probabilities with the Review-1 worked example (N = 10,000).
digit probability percent expected_counts_N_10000
1 0.30103 30.10 3010.3
2 0.17609 17.61 1760.9
3 0.12494 12.49 1249.4
4 0.09691 9.69 969.1
5 0.07918 7.92 791.8
6 0.06695 6.69 669.5
7 0.05799 5.80 579.9
8 0.05115 5.12 511.5
9 0.04576 4.58 457.6

5.2 4.2 Hypotheses and decision rule

\[H_0: \text{the observed first-digit distribution is consistent with the Benford distribution}\] \[H_1: \text{the observed first-digit distribution differs from the Benford distribution}\]

with the Pearson statistic

\[X^2 = \sum_{d=1}^{9} \frac{(O_d - E_d)^2}{E_d}, \qquad \mathrm{df} = 9 - 1 = 8,\]

and \(H_0\) rejected when \(p < \alpha = 0.05\). Two distributions are kept strictly separate throughout: the observed distribution comes from the data, the expected distribution comes from the formula.

5.3 4.3 Validity rules (never silently violated)

  • Reliable - every expected count \(E \ge 5\).
  • Caution - every \(E \ge 1\) and at most 20% of the classes have \(E < 5\) (Cochran’s rule).
  • Not run - any \(E < 1\), or \(N < 50\), or more than 20% of classes with \(E < 5\); the statistic and p-value are returned as NA together with a plain-language reason.

Because the smallest first-digit probability is \(P(9) = 0.04576\), the first-digit test needs \(N \ge 110\) for every expected count to reach 5, and \(N \ge 22\) for every expected count to reach 1. The corresponding thresholds for the first-two-digit and second-digit tests are computed in code from their own probability vectors.

5.4 4.4 Practical deviation measures

Chi-square becomes oversensitive for large \(N\), so every result also reports

  • per-digit observed and expected proportions, their difference and the standardised (Pearson) residual \((O-E)/\sqrt{E}\), with \(|\,\)residual\(| > 1.96\) marked as notable (a screening heuristic);
  • the mean absolute deviation \(\mathrm{MAD} = \frac{1}{9}\sum |p_{\text{obs}} - p_{\text{exp}}|\) with the Nigrini first-digit bands (close conformity \(\le 0.006\), acceptable \(\le 0.012\), marginal \(\le 0.015\), nonconformity above 0.015) - these bands apply to the first digit only, so only the raw MAD is reported for the other digit classes;
  • Cohen’s \(w = \sqrt{X^2/N}\) as the effect size.

5.5 4.5 Multiple testing

Results are grouped into pre-declared families: latest-complete-year cross-sections, pooled country-years, all per-year subsets, and all per-region subsets. Within each family, raw, Holm and Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted p-values are reported and the flags use the BH-adjusted p-value. The family definition is stored in the family column of chi_square_results.csv.

5.6 4.6 Anomaly flag (single decision function)

The flag is one of exactly five categories: not assessed - unsuitable data, not assessed - insufficient sample, statistical deviation: significant AND practically material (adjusted \(p < \alpha\) and MAD above the 0.006 conformity band), statistically significant but small deviation, or no significant deviation detected. Each flag carries a one-sentence interpretation that repeats the boundary statement.

5.7 4.7 Suitability screening

Every column is screened before testing: sample size, dynamic range in orders of magnitude, positive skew, uniqueness, integer/code-like structure, bounded or percentage-like ranges, hard ceilings, heavy rounding and identifier-like column names. Columns that fail are not flagged; they are explained.

7 6. Controlled synthetic manipulation experiment

This part is entirely synthetic (30 replicates per cell). It measures how the first-digit test behaves when a known fraction of records is altered. The control sample is values drawn from \(10^{U(0,6)}\), which conforms to Benford’s Law. Three manipulations are applied to a copy of the control: round-number substitution, leading-digit bias towards digits 5-9, and a multiplicative partial alteration (0.8-1.2x) that is deliberately hard to detect. The true alteration rate is stored in its own column and never mixed with the statistical results.

Detection rate = proportion of replicates with p < alpha. At 0% alteration this is the empirical type-I error rate; it is reported as observed and is not claimed to equal alpha exactly.

7.1 6.1 One-way ANOVA of MAD on the alteration level (BMAT202P Experiment 11)

Unit of analysis: one simulated replicate. Response = MAD, factor = alteration level, separately for each manipulation type (completely randomised design). The slope is the dose-response of the screening measure: for manipulation types that the test can see, MAD rises with the altered fraction. For the partial 0.8-1.2x alteration the slope and R2 are near the noise floor, which is an honest statement about the limits of the method - a small multiplicative change can move MAD very little.

8 7. Interpretation

  • Every first-digit result is reported with its validity tier, so no p-value is quoted outside the conditions under which it is meaningful.
  • Where a significant deviation appears, the practical measures (MAD band, per-digit residuals, Cohen’s \(w\)) decide whether it is material or merely the arithmetic consequence of a large \(N\).
  • The two negative controls (life expectancy and fertility rate) are bounded, narrow-range variables. They deviate strongly and are screened out as unsuitable - the method is discriminating between suitable and unsuitable data, not detecting wrongdoing.
  • Boundary (restated): a statistically significant deviation from Benford’s Law is not proof of fraud, fabrication or manipulation. It is a diagnostic flag for further review. Constrained ranges, psychological price thresholds, caps, rounding and non-multiplicative processes are all legitimate explanations.

9 8. Limitations

  1. Non-independence. The same country appears in many years, so pooled country-year tests are not independent and their p-values are optimistic. The latest-year cross-section is the independent-across-countries unit and is reported alongside.
  2. Aggregates removed. WDI mixes real countries with World / region / income-group aggregates; only rows whose Country Code has a non-empty Region in the country metadata are kept. If the metadata file is missing, the analysis says so instead of guessing.
  3. Bounded and engineered variables. Percentages, shares, indices, land area and life expectancy are not multiplicative-scale quantities, so Benford is the wrong reference for them. The suitability screening and the negative controls make this explicit.
  4. Large-N oversensitivity. With tens of thousands of values, trivial departures become significant; that is why MAD, residuals and Cohen’s \(w\) are always reported.
  5. Rounding and reporting practice. Published figures are rounded and revised; heavy rounding pushes first digits away from Benford.
  6. Benford’s Law is a screening heuristic. It flags unusual digit patterns. It cannot identify who altered what, and it cannot prove intent. Detection rates from the synthetic experiment (0.00-1.00 across levels) show that insensitive alterations can pass unnoticed.

10 9. Conclusion

The pipeline tests the first-digit pattern of every suitable column against the Benford distribution, quantifies the deviation in three independent ways (chi-square p-value with a multiple-testing adjustment, MAD with Nigrini bands, and per-digit Pearson residuals), and flags only those cases that are both statistically significant and practically material. The synthetic experiment shows the method works well against round-number substitution and leading-digit bias once the altered fraction is large enough, and that it is weak against small multiplicative changes. The deliverable is therefore a triage tool: it points at columns and subsets that deserve human review, and it never claims to detect fraud.

Rscript -e "install.packages(c('shiny','bslib','readr','dplyr','tidyr','ggplot2','DT','testthat','rmarkdown','knitr','jsonlite'))"
Rscript scripts/run_all.R
Rscript -e "shiny::runApp('app.R')"
